title: Black Friday for Gold: From the 1869 Crash to Ghana Today | The Long View, Ep. 3
lede: Gold has fallen 36% from its January record, to a 14-month low, as a stronger dollar and the prospect of higher U.S. interest rates bite. The first Black Friday, on September 24, 1869, was also a gold crash. This episode follows the question from Wall Street's gold room to the Gold Coast: when gold breaks, who pays? Plus the week's African markets, three central banks' different calls, Jamaica's rate rise and the dates to watch.
keyPoints: Gold fell to about $3,539 on Nov 20, roughly 36% below its January 28 record of $5,589.38 (Investing News Network).

Fed minutes showed almost all officials saw further rate increases as likely; Ghana cut its policy rate from 14% to 11%; South Africa held at 7.25% on a 4–3 vote (Federal Reserve, Bank of Ghana, EWN).
On Black Friday, Sept 24, 1869, gold fell from $160 to $133 after the Treasury sold $4 million to break Gould and Fisk's corner (Federal Reserve Bank of New York).
Ghana, Africa's top producer, mined a record 6 million ounces in 2025, and gold is about 67% of its export earnings (Reuters, Bank of Ghana).
The Bank of Jamaica raised its policy rate to 6.5% with inflation at 8.2% (Jamaica Gleaner).
